Summary

This paper proposes SyncLLM, a method for converting an autoregressive LLM into a full-duplex spoken dialogue agent that can model overlapping speech, backchannels, and timing-sensitive turn-taking. The core idea is to inject a periodic synchronization mechanism into an LLM by interleaving two speaker streams with speaker/time tokens at fixed chunk intervals, while training on deduplicated HuBERT unit sequences. To address latency, the model predicts both its own next chunk and an estimated user chunk, enabling one-chunk-ahead generation under simulated network delay. The training recipe uses three stages: synthetic turn-based spoken dialogue from text, synthetic full-duplex dialogue without overlaps, and finally real dual-channel spoken dialogue from Fisher. Experiments compare against dGSLM and report substantially better semantic quality, similar or better turn-taking naturalness, and promising simulated interaction under 160–240 ms chunk sizes.

Overall assessment

This is an interesting and ambitious paper on an important problem: moving beyond turn-based voice interfaces toward genuinely synchronous spoken interaction. The paper’s main strengths are the clarity of the problem framing, the practical systems perspective on latency, and the attempt to leverage text-pretrained LLMs for spoken dialogue rather than relying purely on speech-only modeling. The reported gains in semantic meaningfulness over dGSLM are large and, if robust, significant.

At the same time, I have several concerns about evaluation validity, novelty relative to sequence-format engineering plus staged finetuning, and the realism of the “full-duplex interaction” claims. The paper demonstrates strong continuation performance and simulated two-agent interaction, but it does not yet convincingly establish that the system works as a real-time interactive spoken dialogue agent with actual users, streaming ASR/unit extraction, and realistic end-to-end latency budgets. Some methodological details are also missing or underspecified, making it hard to assess reproducibility and the exact source of gains.

I view this as a strong paper in direction and empirical promise, but one that would benefit from tighter claims and stronger validation of the interactive setting.

Strengths

1. Important problem
The paper addresses a real limitation of current spoken dialogue systems: most are effectively turn-based and do not support natural overlap, backchanneling, or timing-sensitive turn exchange. This is a meaningful research direction.

2. Clever synchronization formulation
The use of periodic synchronization tokens to align generation with wall-clock chunks is simple and elegant. The interleaved two-stream representation is intuitive and appears compatible with standard decoder-only LLMs.

3. Practical latency-aware design
The one-chunk delayed-input formulation and explicit prediction of an estimated user chunk is a thoughtful systems contribution. It directly addresses the fact that cloud-hosted models cannot observe the current user chunk instantaneously.

4. Effective use of text-pretrained LLMs
The paper’s strongest empirical message is that leveraging Llama3-8B plus synthetic spoken dialogue yields much better semantic quality than a speech-only baseline. This is plausible and important.

5. Multi-faceted evaluation
The paper includes automatic semantic evaluation, turn-taking statistics, human evaluation, and simulated interaction experiments. This breadth is appreciated.

Weaknesses and concerns

1. The main “full-duplex interaction” claim is only weakly validated
The paper’s title and framing emphasize full-duplex dialogue agents, but the actual evaluation is mostly continuation-based, plus simulated LLM-LLM interaction. This is not the same as demonstrating a deployed interactive agent with real user speech, streaming unit extraction, network jitter, packet delay variation, and actual inference latency.

The interaction setup replaces one stream with another model’s generated stream. That is useful as a simulation, but it avoids several hard issues:
- online speech unit extraction from noisy user audio,
- incremental vocoding and playback,
- synchronization drift,
- ASR/unitization latency,
- user adaptation to system overlap behavior,
- recovery from incorrect predicted user chunks.

As written, the paper somewhat overstates what has been demonstrated.

2. Evaluation of semantics via ASR-transcribed perplexity is indirect
The semantic evaluation converts generated speech to text with ASR, removes overlap, and computes perplexity under a text dialogue model. This is a fairly indirect metric and may be confounded by:
- ASR errors,
- deletion of overlapping content,
- mismatch between spoken dialogue phenomena and text LM perplexity,
- stylistic differences rather than semantic coherence.

The human M-MOS results help, but the automatic semantic metric alone is not fully convincing. It would be stronger to include text-based reference-free dialogue quality metrics, response relevance judgments, or transcript-level human evaluation.

3. Comparison is narrow
The main baseline is dGSLM, which is indeed relevant, but also relatively specialized and older in design assumptions. Since the paper’s main advantage comes from leveraging text-pretrained LLM knowledge, I would have liked stronger baselines such as:
- a cascaded streaming ASR + text LLM + TTS system with explicit turn-taking heuristics,
- a turn-based speech LLM adapted for chunked generation,
- an ablation where Llama3 is trained without synchronization tokens but with similar data,
- a simpler duplex baseline using two independent turn predictors plus response generator.

Without these, it is hard to isolate whether the gains come from “synchronous LLMs” specifically, versus simply using a much stronger pretrained language backbone and much more synthetic data.

4. Novelty is somewhat mixed
The paper’s contribution is partly architectural, but much of the method can also be seen as a sequence formatting and training strategy layered on a standard decoder-only LLM:
- interleaving two streams,
- periodic speaker/time tokens,
- deduplication/interpolation,
- staged synthetic-to-real finetuning.

This is still valuable, but the paper should be more precise about what is fundamentally new algorithmically versus what is an effective engineering recipe.

5. Deduplication/interpolation may distort timing in ways not fully analyzed
The paper argues that deduplication improves semantic density and that interpolation errors are imperceptible. This may be true, but the evidence is limited. Since timing is central to the paper, I would expect:
- quantitative analysis of interpolation error,
- effect on overlap timing,
- effect on pause duration distributions,
- ablation against non-deduplicated modeling or duration-aware tokenization.

The current justification is plausible but under-supported.

6. Human evaluation design has limitations
The MOS study is useful, but there are concerns:
- only 3 raters per item,
- relatively small total item count,
- naturalness and meaningfulness are judged after listening to prompt and continuation, but it is unclear how overlap-heavy samples were presented and whether raters could reliably assess both channels,
- no pairwise preference test,
- no explicit evaluation of interruption appropriateness, backchannel appropriateness, or responsiveness under latency.

Given the paper’s central claims, more targeted human evaluation would be valuable.

7. Missing implementation details and reproducibility gaps
Several details are unclear or absent:
- exact training datasets used in stages 1 and 2,
- total number of samples / turns,
- optimization hyperparameters per stage,
- context length and chunk packing strategy,
- inference-time procedure for replacing predicted user chunks with observed chunks,
- whether KV-cache reuse is used and what the actual runtime latency is,
- vocoder details and whether synthesis is streaming,
- how prompts are selected and how many generations per prompt are used.

These omissions make it difficult to reproduce or fully assess the system.

Detailed comments and questions

1. Real-time feasibility
The paper motivates chunk sizes of 160–240 ms and notes language generation latency around 600 ms in humans/LLMs. But what is the actual end-to-end system latency on realistic hardware?
- unit extraction latency,
- model forward pass latency,
- vocoder latency,
- buffering/playout latency.
Without this, it is hard to know whether the proposed setup is practically deployable.

2. Why is only one speaker tag mandatory?
The sequence format always includes [S0] but may omit [S1] if no novel tokens occur. This asymmetry is clever for chunk delimitation, but does it bias the model toward one speaker as the temporal anchor? Did the authors try alternating anchors or explicit chunk boundary tokens independent of speaker identity?

3. Handling of silence and no-speech chunks
If a chunk contains no novel tokens for either speaker except the mandatory [S0], how often does this happen, and does it create degenerate contexts with many boundary-only chunks? Some statistics would help.

4. Stage 2 synthetic full-duplex without overlaps
This stage is described as modeling timing within utterances but not turn-taking cues. I wonder how much it contributes beyond teaching the sequence format. An ablation removing stage 2 would be informative.

5. Stage 1 mixed text/speech training
This seems important, but the paper gives only a high-level description. What exact text dialogue corpora are used? Are they instruction-following datasets, chat datasets, or multi-turn conversational corpora? The semantic gains may depend heavily on this choice.

6. Evaluation on CANDOR
The OOD results are encouraging, but Fisher and CANDOR differ in more than domain; they may differ in recording conditions, interaction style, and demographics. It would help to discuss what kind of generalization is actually being tested.

7. Turn-taking metric
The paper computes Pearson correlation of average event durations between generations and ground truth. This is a somewhat unusual metric. Correlation of averages may hide substantial distribution mismatch. Why not compare full distributions using Wasserstein distance, KL, or event-level statistics? Also, correlation with the prompt itself is reported, which is interesting, but I am not sure how to interpret it.

8. Missing Figure 7
Figure 7 is marked NOT_FOUND in the provided manuscript text. This should be fixed.

9. Statistical significance
The paper reports confidence intervals for MOS, but significance testing between systems is not clearly stated. Given the strong claims, explicit significance comparisons would help.

10. Safety and misuse
The ethics section is brief. Since the paper enables more human-like spoken interaction, risks include deception, impersonation, and manipulative conversational behavior. These deserve a somewhat fuller discussion.

Suggested ablations

The paper would be much stronger with the following ablations:
- no deduplication vs deduplication,
- no stage 1 / no stage 2 / no stage 3,
- no estimated user chunk at inference,
- chunk size sweep with actual latency-quality tradeoff,
- synchronization token frequency variants,
- text-pretrained LLM backbone vs speech-only backbone under matched data,
- explicit duration modeling vs interpolation heuristic.

Suggested additional evaluations

1. Real interactive demo evaluation with humans
Even a small-scale study where humans converse with the system live would substantially strengthen the paper.

2. End-to-end latency measurements
Report actual wall-clock latency breakdown and throughput.

3. Overlap/backchannel appropriateness
Human judgments specifically on whether interruptions/backchannels occur at appropriate times.

4. Robustness to ASR/unitization noise
If the intended deployment uses live user speech, evaluate with noisy or imperfect online unit extraction.

5. Error recovery
Analyze what happens when the predicted user chunk is wrong. Does the model recover gracefully after replacement with the true chunk?

Clarity and presentation

The paper is generally readable and well motivated. The figures explaining the chunked interleaving are helpful. However, there are many grammatical issues and typos throughout, for example:
- “integrate time information into Llama3-8b so that they run” should be singular/plural consistent,
- “entails model to be always listening”,
- “for help our model learn”,
- “is are almost the same”,
- several duplicated words and formatting inconsistencies.

These do not obscure the main ideas, but the paper would benefit from careful proofreading.

Recommendation

Weak Accept

Rationale

I think this paper presents a compelling direction and a practically meaningful formulation for synchronous spoken dialogue with LLMs. The empirical gains in meaningfulness over dGSLM are substantial, and the synchronization/chunking approach is simple enough to be influential. My main hesitation is that the paper’s strongest claims concern full-duplex interactive dialogue, while the evidence is still mostly continuation-based and simulated. I would encourage acceptance if the venue values forward-looking systems ideas with strong empirical promise, but I also think the authors should moderate claims and strengthen the discussion of limitations.

Confidence

4/5

Questions for the authors

1. What is the actual end-to-end latency of the full system, including unit extraction and vocoding, on realistic hardware?
2. How sensitive are results to the interpolation heuristic after deduplication?
3. How much does stage 2 contribute relative to stages 1 and 3?
4. Can the model recover when its predicted user chunk is substantially wrong?
5. Why was dGSLM chosen as the only main baseline, rather than including a strong cascaded streaming baseline?
6. Are there any live human-agent interaction results, even informal, beyond LLM-LLM simulation?

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper proposes SyncLLM, a method for converting an autoregressive LLM (Llama3-8B) into a full-duplex spoken dialogue agent that can model overlapping speech, backchannels, and latency-tolerant interaction. The core idea is to inject coarse timing via periodic synchronization/speaker tokens and train on interleaved dual-speaker speech-unit sequences, using deduplicated HuBERT tokens for semantic efficiency and interpolation for synthesis. The training recipe uses three stages: synthetic turn-based speech-text alignment, synthetic full-duplex no-overlap dialogue, and finetuning on about 2k hours of real dual-channel dialogue. Experiments against dGSLM show substantially better semantic quality and human-rated meaningfulness, while maintaining comparable naturalness and demonstrating simulated interaction under chunk-based latency up to 240 ms.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: moving from turn-based spoken agents to genuinely synchronous/full-duplex dialogue.
Technically novel framing of synchrony through periodic synchronization tokens and chunked interleaving of two speaker streams within a standard autoregressive LLM.
Practical latency-aware interaction design that explicitly models one-chunk delayed user input and anticipatory prediction.
Strong use of pretrained text LLM knowledge, which plausibly explains the large gains in semantic coherence over speech-only baselines.
Thoughtful data strategy combining large-scale synthetic spoken dialogue with limited real dual-channel speech data.
Empirical results are compelling on meaningfulness: large gains over dGSLM in ASR-based semantic evaluation and human M-MOS.
Includes both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation, suggesting some robustness/generalization.
Human evaluation is reasonably structured and compares against re-synthesized ground truth as a useful topline for the tokenization/vocoder pipeline.
weaknesses: Comparison is primarily against dGSLM; the paper lacks broader baselines such as stronger modern speech-text LLM or cascaded streaming systems.
The key timing representation is fairly coarse, and the interpolation heuristic for reconstructing durations may distort prosody/timing in ways not fully quantified.
The interaction setting is only simulated via LLM-LLM interaction rather than real human-agent deployment, so claims about practical full-duplex usability remain somewhat indirect.
Evaluation of semantics relies on ASR transcription and ignores overlapping speech, which may under-measure full-duplex conversational quality.
Naturalness metrics based on correlation of aggregate turn-taking statistics are informative but limited; they do not fully capture local appropriateness of interruptions/backchannels.
Ablations are limited in the provided text: it is unclear how much each stage, deduplication, chunk size, or anticipation mechanism individually contributes.
The synthetic speech generation process (e.g., Bark with 10 presets) may introduce artifacts or stylistic biases, and the impact of this domain gap is not deeply analyzed.
Speech quality itself is acknowledged as limited, which may constrain real-world user experience despite strong dialogue modeling.
soundness_issues: The methodology is generally coherent, but some central design choices are justified more heuristically than rigorously, especially equal-repeat interpolation within chunks and omission of one speaker tag when no novel token appears.
The semantic evaluation pipeline may confound model quality with ASR errors and transcription choices, especially since overlaps are discarded before text perplexity computation.
The claim of latency tolerance up to 240 ms is supported mainly by simulated chunked interaction rather than end-to-end system measurements with real network/runtime delays.
Human evaluation uses only three raters per item and a relatively small sample size, which is acceptable but limits precision for nuanced naturalness differences.

Because the baseline and proposed system differ in architecture, pretraining regime, and synthetic-data usage, attribution of gains specifically to synchrony modeling versus stronger language priors is not fully isolated.
